title: Microsoft struggles to get M365 services back online after widespread outage
summary: If you’re struggling to send or receive emails, you’re not alone. Microsoft has been unable to fully restore Microsoft 365 more than 13 hours after an Exchange Online failure took down Outlook and spread to Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and parts of the company’s security tooling, and it said overnight that its latest fixes were “not taking as expected.” The outage began at 16:17 UTC on Nov. 12, according to Microsoft’s service health dashboard . “Users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop (MAPI), Exchange ActiveSync (EAS), or REST-based connections, and email delivery may be delayed,” Microsoft wrote in the dashboard. Users in the Americas could not reach their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop Outlook, mobile clients, or the REST API. Within two hours, Microsoft said users in any region could be affected. It opened a wider incident covering Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot, Defender XDR, Intune, Power BI, and several Purview services. Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak. In its latest service-health updates for incident MO1550821 , Microsoft said it had observed a surge in calls from routing services to backend servers as it applied mitigation measures. The company said traffic rebalancing had contributed to the increased volume and that it was scaling virtual machines to add capacity and reduce the load. “As we’ve applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers,” Microsoft said in the update. It added: “We’re continuing to observe heightened volume due to traffic rebalancing actions that we have taken throughout this event.” Server failures behind the disruption Microsoft initially investigated elevated infrastructure load and the possibility that a recent change had contributed to the incident. title: Fei-Fei Li
summary: Fei-Fei Li helped make the visual world a shared resource for artificial intelligence. Her path began with physics at Princeton and doctoral research at Caltech, before leading through university laboratories, ImageNet and the development of spatial models. The images and categories assembled by her collaborators gave researchers a common basis for learning and comparison. They also raised questions about representation and the limits of what a label can tell us about a person. Alongside this scientific work, Li helped establish AI4ALL and Stanford’s institute for human-centred AI, connecting research with education and public responsibility. At World Labs, she and her co-founders are exploring environments that computers can generate and reconstruct. A proposed acquisition by AMD marks another possible transition. Across these settings, her career reveals the people, judgements and institutions behind machine vision, and the continuing challenge of deciding what it means for a computer to understand what it sees.

title: Olmo Hybrid 7B: architecture, evidence and reproducibility
summary: Olmo Hybrid 7B is a research language model from Ai2 that combines recurrent layers with attention. Its relevance extends beyond the availability of its weights: the release connects an architectural hypothesis with published experiments, training materials and a scientific study accepted at COLM 2026. This profile examines what those materials make possible, how the reported efficiency gains should be interpreted, and where reproducibility remains uncertain. It distinguishes the base model from instruction-following and reasoning-oriented variants, separates training infrastructure from practical deployment requirements, and assesses licensing without treating every component as legally interchangeable. The review also considers results that qualify the headline gains and an unresolved discrepancy in the documentation of long-context training. The resulting assessment supports Olmo Hybrid as a valuable object of scientific investigation, while reserving stronger conclusions about general superiority, exact reproduction and reasoning transparency. The Bible of AI (BAI) has not executed the model or independently reproduced its published measurements.

title: Microsoft 365 caught a bug and the whole world sneezed
summary: While Microsoft seems at last to be on the edge of fixing the global outage that hammered its services overnight, causing chaos across Asia-Pacific and Europe, we should still ask: How many times must we endure outages of this kind? How long will it be until government, enterprise, and everyday users understand the need to rely on hybrid systems to drive our digital age, rather than placing complete trust in a single provider? It is, after all, not so very long since the CrowdStrike disaster impacted business users everywhere . This time round we are enduring a massive Microsoft 365 outage that is affecting people across the planet. The problem is that with so many systems reliant on Microsoft’s products, the ripple effect of failure is pressing into adjacent sectors. Police, health services, governments, and all kinds of businesses are facing disruption. One vendor, many casualties Why are they facing this? Because they rely on a single vendor to provide the back end for much of their tech. Even entities you’d imagine wouldn’t be impacted are feeling the pressure. Anthropic has revealed issues with its services. In the UK, the NHS reports that while clinical and operational systems are functioning, communication systems are impacted. At time of writing, the Bank of England has confirmed internal communications issues. All of this chaos is caused by an overreliance on Microsoft. Even new employee onboarding will be impacted, as the outage impacts Intune’ s ability to handle device enrolment, check-in, and compliance. Plus, of course, every third-party system that relies on core Microsoft systems has also failed. It doesn’t need to be this way. Alternatives to Microsoft do exist, and while they may not have captured the business zeitgeist to the same extent as Outlook or Office, in the context of today’s global service disaster, it makes sense for every business to invest more in those alternatives. “This should be a wake-up call for every organisation. title: Subbarao Kambhampati: planning, explanation and the discipline of verification
summary: Subbarao Kambhampati studies what makes a plan workable and an explanation useful. His career connects doctoral research on adapting plans with temporal planning, collaboration between people and robots, and the evaluation of language models. With collaborators, he developed Sapa, helped formulate explanation as reconciliation between different models of a situation, and contributed to PlanBench. His LLM-Modulo proposal gives language models constructive roles alongside external systems that check their outputs. A professor at Arizona State University and former AAAI president, he received the association’s joint educator award with EAAI in 2025. This biography follows the research behind his criticism of unsupported claims about AI, including studies of self-verification and intermediate model outputs. It also considers the progress his group acknowledges, the assumptions behind formal guarantees and the continuing distinction between obtaining a correct answer and understanding why a system produced it.
author: The Bible of AI

title: AI Logic and Reasoning: Past, Present and Future
summary: What would justify saying that an AI system reasons? This article follows the question from explicit symbolic procedures to learned representations, using Othello as a controlled setting in which a model’s predictions can be checked against a known world. It distinguishes successful behaviour, recoverable internal information and evidence of causal influence. The discussion examines why some apparent jumps in capability depend on the scoring method, what interventions can reveal about a model, and why a written chain of thought is not automatically a faithful explanation. Studies that support structured representations are read alongside work that tests their consistency and exposes dependence on training data. The final section considers human–AI collaboration as an empirical question: combining a person and a model does not guarantee a better result. Drawing on primary scientific studies, the article identifies useful standards for future evaluation without treating current findings as proof of general understanding or consciousness.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Gary Marcus: rules, reasoning and the search for trustworthy AI
summary: Gary Marcus has spent his career asking how a learner can go beyond the examples it has encountered. His research on language development and infant rule learning led to a sustained interest in the structures that support generalisation. In The Algebraic Mind, he explored how neural systems could implement symbolic operations; later, with Ernest Davis and Doug Lenat, he developed proposals connecting learning, knowledge and reasoning. His career also includes founding roles at Geometric Intelligence and Robust.AI, books on human cognition and participation in debates about AI governance. A Professor Emeritus at New York University, Marcus continues to argue for hybrid approaches, including a 2026 paper with Vaishak Belle. This biography follows the scientific origins of that programme, the evidence and objections surrounding it, and the distinction between identifying the limitations of existing systems and demonstrating that an alternative can reliably overcome them.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Danijar Hafner: learning to act through world models
summary: Danijar Hafner studies how artificial agents can learn models of their surroundings and use them to decide what to do. His work connects visual experience, prediction and action through a sequence of collaborative projects, including PlaNet, Dreamer and DayDreamer. These systems investigate planning and behaviour learning inside representations acquired from experience, with experiments ranging from simulated control and Minecraft to physical robots. Hafner completed doctoral research at the University of Toronto with Jimmy Ba, following studies at UCL and the Gatsby Unit and research experience at Berkeley and Google Brain. A former Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind, he was named among MIT Technology Review’s Innovators Under 35 in 2026. His trajectory offers a perspective on artificial intelligence centred on acting in an environment. The distinctions between learning a model, producing plausible predictions and achieving reliable behaviour remain essential to understanding both the significance and the limits of that work.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Pierre-Yves Oudeyer: learning through curiosity
summary: Pierre-Yves Oudeyer studies how a learner chooses what to explore. A research director at Inria and head of the Flowers team, he has connected developmental robotics, computational models of language and intrinsic motivation. His early work investigated how shared speech patterns could emerge among interacting agents. Later studies, developed with collaborators including Frédéric Kaplan and Adrien Baranes, examined curiosity, learning progress and the selection of goals. This research has led to experiments in which robots organise aspects of their own practice, as well as investigations of exploratory methods in simulated scientific environments. Oudeyer’s trajectory offers a perspective on artificial intelligence centred on development and experience. It also includes work on grounding language models through interaction. Across these projects, the central question remains concrete: how can a machine discover which experiences will help it learn, within the structures and constraints supplied by its designers?
author: The Bible of AI

title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
summary: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said . This report, based on a survey of 753 cloud decision-makers and users, argues that enterprise cloud has entered a “value era” in which organizations are measuring success less by cost savings alone and more by business outcomes. The headline findings are familiar. Flexera says 64% of organizations now use “value delivered to business units” as a metric for cloud progress, up 12 percentage points year over year. Use of unit economics rose from 40% to 49%. Generative AI usage as a public cloud service rose to 58%, making it one of the most widely used public cloud services in the survey. Meanwhile, 71% of respondents say their company has a cloud center of excellence or a similar team, and 63% say they have a finops team. These reports provide a decent temperature check of what cloud teams are thinking about. The problem is what happens next. A survey of cloud-involved people becomes a story about the market. title: Google adds multi-model Orchestrator, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, to Antigravity
summary: Google is adding a new feature, Orchestrator, to Antigravity, its AI-powered development environment, to help enterprises improve software development efficiency by automatically coordinating multiple Gemini models, including the newly introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen. The new feature, which allows developers to delegate planning, coding, and review tasks to different models within a single coding session, combines a planning model, such as Gemini 4 Carbon or Argon, with Hydrogen, which the hyperscaler describes as a lighter execution model. While the planner models explore the codebase, identify dependencies, and develop an implementation plan, Hydrogen handles execution, including editing files, writing code, and running builds and tests, the hyperscaler wrote in a blog post . That execution differs from conventional model routing, which typically selects a model based on a prompt and assigns it the entire task. Orchestrator, instead, transfers control between the planning and execution models as work progresses, with the planning model first exploring the codebase, identifying dependencies, resolving ambiguities, and preparing an implementation plan before handing control to Hydrogen for execution, the hyperscaler explained in the feature’s documentation . Hydrogen hands control back to the planner if it encounters problems, such as repeated test failures or unexpected behavior, allowing the latter to reassess the execution and revise the plan before Hydrogen resumes implementation, according to the documentation. These handoffs, the hyperscaler said, happen automatically within a single response, without developers having to manually switch models or configure the transitions. title: I spent the last year working in Palantir Foundry... and now I'm back to Snowflake
summary: Palantir Foundry... two words that just might get you crucified around here. At least... they seem to bring out the worst in people on this sub and I kind of see why and also kind of don't. I spent the last 11 months or so working in Foundry and just recently made the jump back into the Snowflake ecosystem... which, for the record, I'm very happy about. That said, I think people around here often misunderstand what Foundry is and is trying to do. Yes, it's a platform or ecosystem and yes there are a lot of "gotchas" and weird/odd things about the platform but it's not truly a DE tool. It's a full-stack tool... that's abstracted. Yes, there are DE related features (python data pipelines, code repositories, git integration) but at its core Foundry is about letting the business make decisions based on ingested data and then write back those decisions to a dataset of some sort. Honestly, it's a unique platform. There's nothing out there, to my knowledge, that does exactly what it does (and yes, its costs and arm and a leg too but... again... nothing does quite what it does). Why did I go back to Snowflake you ask? Well... most of my career (thus far) has been spent in some aspect of data warehousing or data modeling so Snowflake feels like home to me. I think if I had spent more time writing python or working in the full-stack realm Foundry might feel more familiar to me (or maybe not), but ultimately I like working on the backend. Realistically though, I don't see Palantir and Snowflake as direct competitors. Foundry is about decision making, Snowflake, while it's moving in that direction (all the big players are from what I can tell), is ultimately still a data warehouse with a lot of different capabilities that stem from being a high powered OLAP DB. That's probably too simplistic of a synopsis but it's the way I currently see these tools. Anyways, I thought I'd poke the bear and see if others had thoughts (or questions) as well. submitted by /u/SeaYouLaterAllig8tor
